title: Air India Turnaround Could Take a Decade, Tata Sons Chief Warns as Losses Double to $2.3 Billion
excerpt: Tata Sons Chairman N. Chandrasekaran extends the airline's transformation timeline to five to ten years, citing supply-chain disruptions, legacy systems, and the fallout from last year's fatal crash.
body:
• Tata Sons Chairman N. Chandrasekaran has told shareholders that Air India's turnaround should be viewed as a "five to ten year journey," extending the timeline beyond the original five-year Vihaan.AI plan launched in 2022.
  • Air India reported a net loss of ₹22,238 crore ($2.32 billion) for FY26, more than double the ₹10,859 crore loss in FY25, amid airspace closures, elevated fuel costs, and the June 2025 crash of flight AI171.
  • CEO Campbell Wilson is set to step down on September 30, and Tata Sons has not yet announced a successor. Chandrasekaran has been personally overseeing weekly operations reviews.
  • Despite the setbacks, narrow-body fleet refurbishment is complete, and the airline's order for nearly 470 aircraft — one of the largest globally — is expected to begin deliveries from 2027.

Extending the Timeline

Tata Sons Chairman N. Chandrasekaran has acknowledged that turning around Air India will take far longer than originally planned, telling shareholders in the company's FY26 annual report that the airline's transformation "must be seen as a five to ten year journey."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=UJTr-nMMLQM

The admission marks a significant departure from the Vihaan.AI five-year transformation plan unveiled in September 2022 by then-CEO Campbell Wilson, which had set ambitious targets across fleet modernization, customer experience, and network expansion. Three-and-a-half years into that plan, the airline's losses have widened rather than narrowed.

"Given where it began, Air India's transformation must be seen as a five to ten year journey."

— N. Chandrasekaran, Chairman, Tata Sons

Chandrasekaran cited persistent supply-chain disruptions in aircraft components, the need to overhaul legacy technology systems, cultural transformation, fleet modernization, and the effort to build a larger technical and airline workforce as key factors extending the timeline.

Losses More Than Double

Air India reported a net loss of ₹22,238 crore ($2.32 billion) for the financial year ended March 2026, more than double the ₹10,859 crore loss recorded the previous year. The widening losses reflect what Chandrasekaran described as "the most challenging year for Air India."

Three external headwinds hit the airline simultaneously during FY26: airspace closures due to geopolitical tensions, elevated fuel prices driven by the West Asia conflict and foreign exchange fluctuations, and the crash of Air India flight AI171 on June 12, 2025 — a Boeing 787 incident that triggered intensified regulatory oversight, fleet inspections, and scrutiny of operational processes.

The airline temporarily suspended six international routes, including Delhi-Chicago, Delhi-Shanghai, and Mumbai-New York JFK, and reduced frequencies across North American, European, Australian, and Southeast Asian services between June and August 2026. Phased fuel surcharge increases were introduced on domestic and international routes.

Leadership Transition

The turmoil also led to the departure of CEO Campbell Wilson, who is set to step down on September 30 after serving his notice period. Tata Sons has not yet announced a successor.

In the interim, Chandrasekaran has begun personally overseeing weekly reviews of flight operations, commercial strategy, and financial planning. The chairman has directed a "relentless focus on costs," including reducing discretionary spending, reviewing vendor contracts, and deferring non-essential expenditure. Annual salary increments have been postponed by at least one quarter, though the airline has said it does not anticipate layoffs.

What NRI Travelers Should Know

For the Indian diaspora, Air India's extended turnaround timeline has practical implications. The route suspensions and frequency reductions on key corridors to North America, Europe, and Australia mean fewer direct options from India's largest carrier on the routes NRIs fly most frequently.

On the positive side, the airline's massive order for nearly 470 aircraft from Airbus and Boeing is expected to begin deliveries from 2027, which should improve fuel efficiency, reduce maintenance costs, and support network restructuring. Refurbishment of the narrow-body domestic fleet is complete, while wide-body cabin retrofits will continue through late FY28.

India's airline industry has rebounded strongly since the pandemic, but profitability across the sector remains under pressure from high costs, supply-chain constraints, and fierce price competition from carriers like IndiGo.

Looking Ahead

Tata Sons said insurance is expected to cover most of the financial impact from the AI171 crash, with claims from passengers, crew, and third parties largely covered under aviation liability insurance. The FY26 annual report showed Air India recognized a ₹270 crore exceptional item linked to the insurance settlement for the loss of the aircraft.

The carrier has also launched new initiatives to strengthen connectivity, including its "Easy Connect" hub-and-spoke service from regional cities. But industry observers note that Air India's immediate challenge extends beyond managing temporary disruptions — it must ensure operational restructuring keeps pace with the scale of its long-term expansion plans.
nri_angle: NRI travelers face reduced Air India options on key North American, European, and Australian corridors during the extended turnaround, though new aircraft deliveries from 2027 promise improved service.
